rules.statement: Let an OperationCanceledException raised by the caller's cancellation token escape as is, rather than wrapping it in a domain exception, and document that a call already sent may still take effect.
rules.why: OperationCanceledException is the cancellation signal in the primitives' contracts, after which a write's outcome is unknown; translating it into another exception type would break that contract.
rules.check: Look for catch blocks that turn an OperationCanceledException from the caller's token into a custom exception. Don't report code that lets it propagate. Do check that the `<exception>` docs say the outcome is unknown after cancellation.

rules.statement: Don't catch InvalidCastException as control flow when converting a value of unknown shape: check its type or null state first, and name the actual type in the failure message.
rules.why: Catching the cast exception hides other cast failures behind one generic message, and operators can't tell what was actually returned without a debugger.
rules.check: Look for try/catch around a cast or conversion that catches InvalidCastException and falls back to null or a generic error, and for error messages that don't say what type of value was received.

rules.statement: Don't report a `//` comment that cites an ADR next to a member's XML doc block: the C# conventions put ADR citations in `//` comments because `///` docs never cite an ADR.
rules.why: The conventions keep ADR references out of public XML docs and put them in plain comments that point to where the reason is recorded.
rules.check: Before reporting a stray ADR reference, check whether it is a `//` comment rather than `///` text. Only `///` citations of ADRs break the convention.

rules.statement: Don't report that an ADR's record of an observed run names a newer dependency version than the pinned or minimum version, when the pin comes from the dependency cooldown policy.
rules.why: The observation records the run as it happened. The pinned version and the minimum come from the cooldown policy, and CI tests run on the pinned version.
rules.check: Before reporting a version mismatch in an ADR's Observed notes, check whether the lower pinned or minimum version is set by the dependency cooldown policy and whether CI tests cover the pinned version.

rules.statement: When an options type accepts a client or connection supplied and owned by the host, document in its `<remarks>` (and in the package README) which of that client's settings the library relies on and what happens if they differ.
rules.why: A host passing its own shared client otherwise gets no warning that its settings affect how the library behaves, for example how failures are classified.
rules.check: Look for new or changed option properties that take a shared external client or connection, with docs that only cover ownership or disposal and don't name the required settings.

rules.statement: A parameter's doc must state exactly what the type disposes, and must say when an injected resource that the type doesn't own is left undisposed.
rules.why: A loose doc such as 'which the provider disposes' makes readers think the type tears down a shared resource owned by the host.
rules.check: Compare `<param>` and remarks docs about disposal with the actual Dispose logic, especially when ownership depends on a flag such as `owned`.

rules.statement: When a type's get-only properties are initialized from primary-constructor parameters or static fields, order the initializers so that guards and dependencies run before their users, because initializers run in textual order.
rules.why: Field and property initializers run in declaration order, so a hoisted static field or guarded parameter must come before the initializers that use it.
rules.check: Look for property or static field initializers that use another static field or guarded value declared below them.

rules.statement: Don't report a bool parameter on an internal method under the flag-parameter rule: that rule covers public API, and a bool that carries a fact the method reads as data, named at every call site, is allowed.
rules.why: The flag-parameter rule sits in the Public API section of the C# conventions, and the same rule allows a bool carried as data.
rules.check: Before reporting a flag parameter, check whether the member is public and whether call sites pass the bool as a named argument that describes a fact.

rules.statement: Don't report a public constructor for having more than three parameters when every parameter is a required input: the conventions make required inputs constructor parameters, and 'rarely more than three' is guidance, not a ban.
rules.why: The Public API conventions put required inputs in the constructor, and changing it to a settings record or `required init` would change the public API for a nit.
rules.check: Before reporting a long constructor, check whether all its parameters are required and whether a misordered call would be caught some other way, such as validation at startup.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask for a shared base test class for the strict MockRepository: a test class that owns its own repository and verifies it on dispose meets the convention.
rules.why: The test conventions ask only that mocks come from one MockRepository that the test class verifies on dispose; a base class is an example, not a requirement.
rules.check: Before reporting duplicated mock setup, check that each test class creates one MockRepository and calls Verify in Dispose. If it does, don't report it.

rules.statement: Don't ask an internal wrapper to take read-only collection interfaces instead of arrays when it passes them straight to a client API that requires arrays and never writes to them.
rules.why: Taking an interface would force a copy at the client call, and passing the caller's arrays through unchanged avoids that copy.
rules.check: Before reporting array parameters under the read-only collection rule, check whether the member is internal, whether the arrays go unchanged to an API whose signature needs arrays, and whether anything writes to them.
